author: blu
body: That second case is what miscompiled hexwar-loop. Five parameters leave the fifth in a spill slot, which makes its argument the complex one; three of the remaining arguments were spilled locals; the third of those loads reclaimed the register holding the fifth argument, and the parameter was assigned the fourth argument's value instead of its own. The counter it drove then stopped advancing. Pinned by codex/test/tco-shuffle-spill.

author: blu
body: That is not a hypothesis. Built with accum-capacity at 16, the compiler emits a factorial whose call-patch target is the EMPTY STRING, and the only thing that notices is CDX2040 reporting an unresolved call to ''. At the real capacity the same corruption waits for a unit large enough to reach it, and the diagnostic it would produce names nothing.

author: blu
body: So this is checked before each function rather than discovered after. It was written to be, and was never called -- a guard defined and left unwired is worth exactly as much as no guard, and reads like a promise that the capacity is watched. ArchitectsSketchbook said it was.

author: blu
body: A proof erases, and CDX4020 says so on the way past it below. That was fine while every definition reached the emitter, and whole-program dead code elimination ended it: a proof is not reachable from `opening`, so the prune drops it, the emitter never sees it, and the diagnostic went silent. Nothing unsound got through and nothing about the checking changed, but five tests stopped seeing the code they pin.

author: blu
body: The instruction count is a decode of the function's finished bytes (x86-count-insns), taken after emit-function has applied its NOP compaction, so the reported CDX6010 count is the count the machine executes. A negative count is the decoder's undecodable-byte report: the emitter produced an encoding outside the decode vocabulary, and the honest response is CDX6012 rather than a partial number.

author: blu
body: The budget that was never checked at all. emit-wcet-check above runs per EMITTED body, so a punctual definition the inliner absorbed into its callers, or one nothing ever calls, is dropped by the emit-time prune and reaches this code never: CDX6010 and CDX6011 both go silent and the author's declared budget is enforced by nothing. Measured against seed EFC7FCD0, a five-instruction body declaring a budget of two raises CDX6011 with the inliner off and nothing at all under the default pipeline.

author: blu
body: The clause body is a binding region and restores the locals prefix it started from. The two binders here are NOT the same and must not be treated the same.

author: blu
body: `resume-name` belongs to the clause body alone. It leaked into the next clause, into the handled expression, and past the `with` -- and the type checker never agreed (`infer-handle-clauses` binds it into a fresh env and hands the ORIGINAL env to the next clause), nor did the resolver (`resolve-handle-clauses` forks per clause). So a later read of that word type-checked against the outer binding and loaded the clause's slot, which by then had been recycled: a silent miscompile that CRASHES NOTHING and prints a plausible wrong answer.

author: blu
body: Each of the three regions is a binding region and restores the locals prefix it started from. A `x <- e` in the body used to stay bound in the fallback, in the on-failure block, and after the end -- and the type checker never agreed, because `infer-act` is handed the untouched env per region. So a fallback naming the same word as an outer binding type-checked against the OUTER one and loaded the BODY's slot: a silent miscompile of the shadowed-let class, not a diagnostic.

author: blu
body: That was a silent wrong answer, not a crash: a call of the shape `f (r.field) ("some literal") (n) (list-length r.field)` compiled the last argument into a read of the LITERAL's length word, so `list-length [7, 8, 9]` returned 9 -- the character count of "read-text". Pinned by codex/test/field-cache-text-lit. It first surfaced where the bogus length sent find-effect-op-addr walking off the end of a 2-element list into a non-canonical pointer; the crash only appeared when the heap layout happened to put something unreadable there, and every other program simply got the wrong number. emit-load-from-handler-table already evicts RAX and R11 for exactly this reason -- this function was the one that forgot.

author: blu
body: This is the third site on this axis, after arithmetic on a unit Real emitting integer arithmetic and `==` on a unit Text comparing pointers. The map is `strip-unit-ty`'s callers.

author: blu
body: Both modes trapped on NaN and did nothing whatever about infinity, which is half of what each is for. Nothing could see it: `real-trapping` adds 3 and 4, and `real-saturating` adds 3 and 4 and then divides zero by zero. Neither test ever produced a value outside the finite range, so both exercised the arithmetic and never the mode.

author: blu
body: A `unit` type is a wrapper codegen erases, so what a comparison must dispatch on is what is INSIDE it. Both fused guards above already unwrap one level and accept only Integer, Boolean or Char within a unit; this arm matched `RealTy` directly, so a `unit Real` resolved to `UnitTy(RealTy)`, matched neither floating arm, and went to the integer comparator -- the same defect the four scalar operators had, one type wrapper deeper and on a path nothing in the tree exercised. `cdx-int-compare-on-float` caught it instead of letting it emit, which is what that guard exists for.

author: blu
body: `strip-unit-ty` used to be defined here. It is in `Types chapter Codex Types` now, because lowering needs the same answer and a second copy of it would drift from this one exactly as the other copies already had.

author: blu
body: It sits on the ORDERING path only. Equality is a different question with a real answer: `emit-eq-op` has its own TextTy arm calling `__str_eq`, and nothing here touches it.

author: blu
body: Did the code emitted so far end in an unconditional jump? st-append-code records where the last one ended; see the note there for why this cannot be read back out of the buffer.

author: blu
body: `^` had NO arm in the dispatch above at all. It fell to the catch-all, which returns `reg-rax` without emitting anything, so the operator handed back whatever happened to be in that register: `2 ^ 3` answered 1130508, a code address. The `__ipow` helper has been emitted into every binary this compiler has ever produced and nothing has ever called it.

author: blu
body: The unit wrapper is stripped first, for the reason `strip-unit-ty`'s own prose gives: a `unit Real` is a Real at runtime and dispatching on the wrapper is how three separate defects got in.

author: blu
body: The unit wrapper is stripped before the dispatch, exactly as emit-ord-comparison and emit-pow-op strip it, and for the same reason: a `unit Text` is a Text at runtime, and a dispatch that reads the wrapper falls to the `otherwise` arm and compares two ADDRESSES.

author: blu
body: The SumTy arm had the same hole and it is closed by the same strip: a unit over a sum type was getting a pointer compare where a structural one was meant.

author: blu
body: emit-ord-comparison twenty lines up already HALTS on a Text operand, saying a machine cmp on Text follows allocation order rather than content. The ordering path has guarded this since it was written; the equality path was quietly doing it.

author: blu
body: The unit arm here used to be spelled out one level deep, which is the fifth copy of a strip `strip-unit-ty` exists to prevent and which a `unit` over a `unit` walks straight past. It reads the shared derivation now; for a single wrapper the answer is unchanged.
